days.content:
Avalanches are possible in the mountains of Colorado whenever you find snow on a steep slope. Consider the consequences of being caught in an avalanche before crossing any steep, snow-covered slopes, even in the spring and summer.

Start and end your day early to avoid wet snow avalanches. Steer clear of steep, rocky snow-covered terrain, especially if the snowpack does not freeze the night before. You can check current weather conditions, including overnight temperatures, on the CAIC Weather Station page.

Wet avalanches are more likely when the surface snow is wet and slushy. These conditions are common after about 10:00 AM this time of year, but you should pay more attention to the snow surface than the time of day. If you find more than a few inches of wet, gloppy snow at the surface, sink past your boot tops into wet unconsolidated snow, feel the surface crusts collapse, or see avalanches running from steep rocky terrain, it's time to find a cooler, more supportable snowpack or call it a day. Most avalanches are relatively small this time of year, but small avalanches can entrain enough wet snow to knock you down and send you for a dangerous ride. 

Avoid travel under sagging and overhanging cornices and stay well back from the edge if you are traveling along ridgelines. 

Learn more about spring and summer avalanche safety here.

title: Front Range, Never Summer, Gore, and Summit SAA
Southern Mountains Regional Discussion
message:
Southern Mountains Regional Discussion

Warming and sunshine could bring wet-snow hazards back into play in the afternoon, but in many areas, the snow is slowly melting. Over the coming days, we will be in a melt-freeze cycle. See the advice below for more on this.

Navigating Spring's Predictable Avalanche Patterns

Spring in the mountains brings longer days, warmer temperatures, and often a welcome reprieve from managing mid-winter Persistent Slab avalanche problems. Instead, we can expect a fairly predictable, fast-changing pattern of repeating avalanche concerns. The four basic elements of the spring avalanche pattern include: Melt-Freeze Cycles, Gouging Wet Avalanches during warm spells, Storm Cycles, and Shed Cycles. By recognizing which moment in time you are at amongst this pattern, you can make safer, smarter decisions in the backcountry.

Consequences of Small Avalanches

While many avalanches in the spring are relatively small, it is critical not to underestimate them, especially if you choose to travel in extreme or high-consequence terrain. A small Loose Wet avalanche, or a Loose Dry sluff, may not bury you, but if it pushes you over a cliff, or drags you through rocks, the consequences can be fatal. The forecast often warns specifically against the destructive consequences of even small avalanches in terrain traps or near high-exposure features. Always assess the terrain below you, even for a slide you think is minor.

The Melt-Freeze Cycle

The backbone of safe spring avalanche conditions is a solid overnight re-freeze of a previously wetted snow surface.  

To recognize these conditions in the days ahead, look for a forecast for clear skies and mid-mountain low temperatures in the 20s. Start early, and plan to end early. Test the quality of the freeze by jumping on the snow. If you barely penetrate the snow surface, you’ve got a good window of safe avalanche conditions ahead. If you punch through a thin frozen layer, your window of opportunity may not last that long.

Once warmth and sun melt the snow surface, wet avalanches become your primary concern. As you travel into different terrain and as time passes, monitor the strength of the snow surface by continuing to jump on it in your boots. How deeply you penetrate the snow surface indicates how deeply a Loose Wet avalanche might gouge. Once you’re past ankle deep, it’s time to consider moving off or out from under steep terrain. Sometimes moving to north-facing terrain can extend your window of opportunity.

Gouging Wet Avalanches

The melt-freeze cycle relies entirely on a good overnight freeze. When overnight temperatures stay near or above freezing, or cloud cover inhibits radiational cooling, the snow doesn't freeze as well, if at all. Under these conditions, be aware of the potential for more dangerous, full-depth gouging wet avalanche activity. When you jump on the snow and you quickly punch through the snow surface into wet snow below the surface crust, you’ve found the concerning “trap-door” setup. These slides can entrain a lot of wet snow, making them significantly more destructive. Your window for safe travel may be short in the morning hours or nonexistent. More non-freezing nights in a row aggravate the problem, but one solid freeze that leads into cooler weather can stop the pattern in its tracks.

The Winter Interruption: Storm Cycles

Just when you settle into your spring routine, winter-like storms can interrupt the melt-freeze cycle with a fresh blanket of dry snow on top of the old melt-freeze surface. When new snowfall arrives, your primary concerns are avalanches in the new and drifting snow. The time of day when the storm starts, and whether the new snow falls on a melted or frozen surface, will impact how well the new snow bonds to the old.

During and just after the storm Dry Loose and Wind Slab avalanches are the most common problems. Use different tactics in the terrain to manage these problems. Dry Loose avalanches flush easily on slopes steeper than about 40 degrees. Choose ridges or higher ribs in the terrain, and stay away from plunging gullies where snow funnels. Avoid triggering a Wind Slab avalanche by steering around denser, wind-drifted snow. If the new snow is more than about a foot deep, especially if it feels “upside-down” or denser on top, consider the potential to trigger a terrain-feature-wide Storm Slab avalanche.

The Post-Storm "Shed Cycle"

Once the storm clears and the sun returns, or temperatures rise well above freezing, the new snow immediately begins to get wet. The transition from dry powder to a quick shed cycle of Loose Wet avalanches can occur in tens of minutes. Evidence of the fast-arriving change usually starts first below sun-warmed east-facing cliffs. Look for clumps of wet snow pinwheeling into cinnamon rolls. “Hot pow” or sticky moist snow soon gives way to a natural cycle of wet avalanches. These increase in size proportionally to the depth of the once-dry new snow - a bigger, colder storm will produce a bigger shed if followed by a rapid warm up (think the day after a transient cold front). The faster and more dramatic the melt rate, the more avalanches you can expect. After a day or two of shedding, the Melt-Freeze Cycle begins again.

Timing Matters

Keep an eye on the overnight temperatures. Observe the timing and impact of intense spring sunshine (jump on the snow). Anticipate how a fresh storm changes your avalanche concerns, and you can predict and prepare for spring avalanche conditions. Travel smart, travel early, and enjoy the longer days safely.

Images.caption: While the recent snowfall wasn't enough to increase the avalanche danger, we could see some Loose Wet avalanches later in the week. Most of the avalanches reported recently have been loose, but some have gouged into slabs like the area in the middle of this photo.
Wet snow avalanches that run through couloirs could lead to a nasty ride. Make sure to assess the slopes you travel, especially in high-consequence terrain.

With a warming trend later in the week, we could see a small uptick in Loose Wet avalanche activity. Pay attention to signs of warming snow and move out from under steep rocky slopes if you see warming signs.
Images.altText: small roller balls on steep slope
